content: Flax, also known as Common Flax or Linseed, belongs to the genus Linum within the family Linaceae. It is distinct from the New Zealand flax, which is unrelated. Flax is indigenous to a region spanning from the eastern Mediterranean to India and was likely first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent. Historically, it was widely cultivated in ancient Egypt. The plant can grow up to 2 meters tall, with slender stems. Its leaves are glaucous green, narrow, and lance-shaped, measuring 20-40 mm in length and 3 mm in width. The flowers are pale blue, 15-25 mm in diameter, and consist of five petals. The fruit is a round, dry capsule, 5-9 mm in diameter, containing several glossy brown seeds shaped like apple pips, each 4-7 mm long. The term flax can also refer to the unspun fibers derived from the plant. Flax is cultivated for both its seeds and fibers. Various parts of the plant have been utilized to produce fabric, dye, paper, medicines, fishing nets, and soap. It is also grown as an ornamental plant in gardens, as it is one of the few species capable of producing truly blue flowers, although not all flax varieties exhibit this trait. Flax seeds yield a vegetable oil known as linseed oil or flaxseed oil, one of the oldest commercial oils. Solvent-processed linseed oil has been used for centuries as a drying oil in painting and varnishing. Flax seeds are available in two primary varieties: brown and yellow (also called golden). While brown flax is edible and has been consumed for thousands of years, it is more commonly associated with industrial uses such as paints, fibers, and cattle feed. Both brown and yellow flax varieties have similar nutritional profiles, including equivalent amounts of short-chain omega-3 fatty acids. However, a specific type of yellow flax called solin (or Linola) is notably low in omega-3 and has a distinct oil profile. A new yellow flaxseed variety called Omega, developed through research at North Dakota State University, was created primarily as a food source. It has a nutty-buttery flavor and contains omega-3 fatty acids comparable to brown flax. Ground flax seeds can serve as an egg substitute in baking by mixing one tablespoon of ground seeds with three tablespoons of water, which acts as a binding agent. They can also be incorporated into oatmeal, yogurt, water, or other foods where a nutty flavor is desirable. Flaxseed oil is commonly consumed with salads or in capsule form. The nutritional benefits of flaxseed are attributed to lignans and omega-3 essential fatty acids. Omega-3s, often deficient in populations with low fish consumption, support cardiovascular health by reducing cholesterol, blood pressure, and arterial plaque formation. Flaxseed oil is also frequently recommended as a galactagogue. However, excessive consumption of flax seeds may lead to diarrhea. Lignans in flaxseed contribute to heart health and exhibit anti-cancer properties. Research led by Lilian U. Thompson and colleagues at the University of Toronto's Department of Nutritional Science has demonstrated that flaxseed can reduce tumor growth in mice, particularly in cases of post-menopausal breast cancer. These effects are believed to be due to the lignans in flaxseed and are additive when combined with tamoxifen. Preliminary studies suggest similar benefits in human cancer patients, including those with prostate cancer. Additionally, flax may help stabilize blood sugar levels, potentially reducing the severity of diabetes. Flaxseed sprouts are edible and have a slightly spicy flavor. Flaxseed is also known as linseed and is referred to by various names in different languages, such as San or Alsi in Hindi, Gujarati, and Punjabi, Ali Vidai in Tamil, Jawas or Alashi in Marathi, Tishi in Bengali, Pesi in Oriya, Agasi in Kannada, Avise ginzalu in Telugu, and Cheruchana vithu in Malayalam. Flax fibers are among the oldest fiber crops globally, with their use in linen production dating back 5,000 years. Ancient Egyptian tombs and temple walls at Thebes depict flowering flax plants. In northern Europe, flax fiber was used for cloth production during Neolithic times. The Puritans introduced flax to North America. Today, most flax produced in the USA and Canada is of the seed flax type, used for linseed oil production or human nutrition. Flax fiber is extracted from the bast or skin of the plant's stem. It is soft, lustrous, and flexible, stronger than cotton fiber but less elastic. The highest-quality grades are used for linen fabrics like damasks, lace, and sheeting, while coarser grades are used for twine and rope. Flax fiber is also a raw material for high-quality paper, including banknotes and cigarette rolling paper. Flax mills for spinning flaxen yarn were invented by John Kendrew and Thomas Porthouse of Darlington in 1787. Major fiber flax-producing countries include Canada, the USA, and China, with significant production also occurring in India and Europe. Flax thrives in deep, friable loams rich in organic matter, while heavy clays and gravelly or dry sandy soils are unsuitable. Flax farming requires minimal fertilizers or pesticides. Under optimal growth conditions, the plant reaches 10-15 cm in height within six weeks of sowing and grows several centimeters daily, reaching 70-80 cm within 15 days. Flax is harvested for fiber production approximately 100 days after sowing, a month after flowering, and two weeks after seed capsule formation. The plant's base turns yellow, indicating readiness for harvest. If harvested too early, the seeds are unusable, and the fiber is underdeveloped. Overripe plants result in degraded fiber. Mature plants are uprooted to maximize fiber length, dried, and then retted to separate the fibers. Retting involves enzymatic degradation of pectins binding the fibers to the straw. This process can take 2 weeks to 2 months, depending on climatic conditions and flax characteristics. Farmers turn the straw during retting to ensure even processing. Once retted and dried, the straw is rolled up and stored before scutching to extract fibers. Flax grown for seed is allowed to mature until the seed capsules turn yellow and begin to split, after which it is harvested using a combine harvester and dried to extract the seeds. Threshing is the process of removing seeds from the plant. It involves machines for threshing seeds, breaking and separating wood from fiber, and further refining the fiber. Farmers may thresh seeds in their own mills, eliminating the need for the first machine. The second part of the process, intended for manufacturers, involves refining the flax for fine purposes like lace, cambric, damask, and fine linen. This is done using a refining machine. Before spinning flax fibers into linen, they must be separated from the stalk through a process called retting, which rots away the inner stalk while leaving the outer fibers intact. The straw is then broken into small bits, scutched to scrape away straw from the fiber, and pulled through hackles to comb out remaining straw. Retting can be done in ponds, streams, fields, or containers. Pond retting is the fastest method but may result in lower-quality fibers and produces an odor. Stream retting takes longer but yields cleaner fibers with less odor. Field retting, which involves laying flax in a field to collect dew, is considered the best method for high-quality fibers and produces minimal pollution. Retting can also be done in watertight containers, but metal containers are unsuitable due to corrosion caused by acids produced during retting. Dressing flax involves breaking, scutching, and hackling to remove straw from the fibers. Breaking breaks up the straw, scutching scrapes away straw, and hackling combs out remaining straw. Flax is a symbolic image in various cultures. It is the national flower of Belarus, the emblem of the Northern Ireland Assembly, and appeared on the reverse of British one-pound coins minted in 1986 and 1991 to represent Northern Ireland. In English, blond hair is traditionally referred to as fair or flaxen.
